1	Claudinite self-test: 1 of 5 probes FAILED — skill-links
2	  - skill-links: 1 mounted skill link(s) dangle: .claude/skills/engineering-practices
3	    fix: re-run the skill mount (baselining does it) — a dangling link is a skill the session cannot load (#424)
4	# Claudinite — active-pack guidance
5	
6	The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand.
7	
8	<!-- pack:basics -->
9	# Working discipline
10	
11	The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.
12	
13	Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.
14	
15	Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). **An automation dispatch prompt is a comment too** — classify it, class `other`, in your *first* substantive reply rather than at the end of the run. The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Put the class **alone on that line**: the line is scanned for *every* class token on it, so restating the menu to rule options out ("not a correction, feature request, or process-change") declares all of them, arming the gates those classes carry. Any explanation goes on the next line. This cannot be taken back — the transcript is append-only, and a clean re-declaration further down does not override the first.
16	
17	1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
18	2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
19	3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Put on the ladder only a rule that constrains *how work is done* and outlives any one feature; a checkable signature doesn't earn a rule its place. Reject two shapes outright: a check that asserts particular code exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time — it dies with the code it pins and constrains no later change), and a rule derivable from the product's requirements (that is a requirement — take it to mode 2: the requirements document and the test that proves it). Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.
20	
21	The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.
22	
23	Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided. For release, deploy, versioning or CI plumbing, look for the shared pack that owns it first — copying a mechanic from a sibling repo is the tell that it belongs centrally. If no pack owns it, report the gap rather than authoring a third copy that gets deleted later along with its reviewed workflow.
24	
25	**Minimize every task's shelf-life — the time from starting it until everyone can forget about it.** An open task is a standing tax: whoever returns to it pays a full reload of the context that was free while the work was hot. So finish a change by **watching it work now** — never park it on "check tomorrow", which is almost always the wrong choice in any context. A change to scheduled or unattended machinery does not wait for its next natural run — force one now (the scheduler's `FORCE_TASKS` lever, a `workflow_dispatch`, the fleet-wide force sweep) and watch it to a terminal state; those levers exist precisely so verification can happen while the change is still in someone's head. The same yardstick governs **migration planning**: prefer the design that converges in one forced pass over the one that trickles across nightly cycles, accept legacy input at the door so nothing has to wait for stragglers, and drive the stragglers with a standing mechanism rather than a phase someone must remember to close. When verifying now is genuinely impossible (an external release window, an upstream fix in flight), the follow-up must be a mechanism that comes to you — a scheduled task, a watched PR, an issue something converges — never a human's memory.
26	
27	When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.
28	
29	When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."
30	
31	Three harness-tool contracts, before you spend a call rediscovering them:
32	
33	- **A `ToolSearch` that finds nothing is evidence about your query, not about the environment.** Deferred tools are matched on keywords that aren't their own vocabulary, so a capability can sit in the session while the search denies it. Search the fully-qualified name (`select:mcp__<server>__<tool>`, copied off the deferred-tools listing — the bare short name returns "no matching tools", which reads exactly like absence) and try the tool before telling the owner a step is theirs.
34	- **`Edit` requires the file to have been read *with the read tool*** — `cat`/`grep`/`sed` don't count, however much is already on screen. The moment shell output tells you which file you're about to change, read that exact path; a narrow offset window satisfies it.
35	- **A summarizing fetch tool is not a source.** Asked for exact text it returns a description, and ordinary publisher pages routinely `403`. When the bytes matter, `curl` into the scratchpad and read from disk. On a `403` don't retry and don't try a sibling URL — attribute the search snippet to the publisher instead of asserting it, and mark it for re-verification.
36	
37	Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.
38	
39	Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere. When the finding is on *text* rather than code, try deleting the flagged phrase before waiving it — decoration often buys the coupling the rule exists to prevent for nothing, and a waiver is for a crossing that genuinely must exist.
40	
41	A blocked host is a **policy boundary, not an obstacle to route around**. When a sandbox or proxy denies a fetch, don't reach for an open-network runner — an ad-hoc CI workflow, a push-triggered "probe" — to make the request from somewhere the policy doesn't apply. Answer from committed reference material or ask the owner, and say plainly that anything unverifiable is unverified.
42	
43	Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.
44	
45	When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.
46	
47	An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.
48	
49	# The task lifecycle
50	
51	The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.
52	
53	For every new task:
54	
55	1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
56	2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
57	3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.
58	
59	A step only a human can perform — flipping a repository or console setting, granting a permission, adding a secret — gets **its own issue**, never a note in the PR body: the note merges and disappears with the PR while the setting stays unflipped. Give it a checkbox per step, what breaks while each is off, and its closing condition. The exception is a step whose home is an artifact the human is already editing. Before handing a step over at all, confirm you genuinely can't do it yourself.
60	
61	# Engineering practices
62	
63	General software-engineering practices, independent of any one project — portable, shared rules; project-specific rules (architecture, test mechanics) live in the consuming repo's own docs. The portable git/GitHub-operational practices — branch/commit history, merging, automated-job branches — live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md); the mechanics of searching and rewriting text across files — grep/sed sweeps, renames, broken references — live in [the repo-text-sweeps skill](skills/repo-text-sweeps/SKILL.md); the practices for writing trustworthy tests — see-it-fail, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, coverage gating — live in [the writing-tests skill](skills/writing-tests/SKILL.md); and how to investigate a bug and pin down its root cause — version-gap triage, re-deriving after a failed fix, probing for a real datapoint — lives in [the bug-investigation skill](skills/bug-investigation/SKILL.md).
64	
65	- Name by scope/responsibility, not technology or mechanism.
66	- Keep a single source of truth for derived or duplicated data — generate the rest from it instead of hand-editing, and have a test fail if it drifts. Split a fact across more than one place only when a technological constraint forbids a single home, and then have the drift-guard test state, in its own text, the two-or-more places it watches and why the split is forced — so an invisible coupling becomes a self-documenting, reviewed one, and the next reader knows the duplication is deliberate and where its other half lives. When the duplicate mirrors executable logic you can't generate from (e.g. a static list shadowing a set of predicate/matcher functions), drift-guard it by *executing the real logic* against the list in both directions — every entry accepted by some predicate, and every predicate satisfied by some entry — rather than parsing the logic out. When a value must be copied into files that can't share an import (a label spanning a YAML workflow guard and a JS module; a repo slug in prod code and its test), declare it as a `sharedConstants` entry in `.claudinite-checks.json` — its `value`, the expected per-file `counts`, and a `what` naming the places and why. Declared counts are matched against the *flat* literal (comments included), so keep a guarded value on one line wherever it appears — an occurrence wrapped across a line break is invisible to a `grep`/`sed` rename alike. For a value that must stay in sync but *changes over time* (a version string bumped each release), set `regex: true` and give a pattern instead of a literal — every match must then be identical across the declared files, so the guard never needs re-pinning on a bump.
67	- Honor separation of concerns in what you write — code comments and Markdown instructions alike: when file A uses or references file B (a module A imports, or a doc/procedure set A points to), A may state *what* it needs from B or *that* it delegates to B, but never restate *how* B does its job or re-spell the procedures B owns. B's mechanism lives in one place — with B. Copying it into A leaks B's internals across the boundary and springs the same drift trap as any duplicated source of truth: change B and A's paraphrase silently goes stale, with nothing to catch it. Point to B instead of paraphrasing it.
68	- One commit per concern: two changes that could each stand alone — separately revertible, cherry-pickable, bisectable — don't share a commit, and a message that numbers unrelated items is describing the split it should have been. More commits is not the goal: once a commit is in, later work is a *new* commit, never a rewrite of the one that landed.
69	- Name any file a test autogenerates with `GENERATED` in its filename (e.g. `foo.GENERATED.md`, `foo.baseline.GENERATED.json`) so it's unmistakable at a glance. Don't hand-edit a GENERATED file, and never resolve its merge conflict by hand: take either side to clear the markers, re-run the generator against the merged inputs, and commit its output. Hand-editing desyncs it from its source — and when the other branch changed the generator's logic, only a re-run produces correct values. Automate the "take either side" step itself where you can: assign the file a `merge=ours` `.gitattributes` entry (plus a one-time `git config merge.ours.driver true` per clone) so a conflicting merge on it resolves automatically instead of needing the markers cleared by hand first; `git config rerere.enabled true` similarly replays a manual conflict resolution automatically the next time the same conflict recurs.
70	- Verify how a platform or runtime actually behaves against authoritative docs or a real run — not against a comment or a prior commit's claim.
71	- Prove a *behaviour-preserving* optimisation actually preserves behaviour before trusting it — "it should be equivalent" is not evidence. Fingerprint the full outputs (hash them) and exercise the old and new paths across *every* branch (fuzz the inputs that select each), accepting the change only on a bit-identical match. And it is legitimate to leave a hot path un-optimised when the correctness risk of rewriting it outweighs the speed-up — record that as a deliberate call, not an oversight.
72	- Earn each dependency: prefer a built-in (or a few lines) for a narrow job, and drop one when the assumption that justified it lapses.
73	- Before adding production code for a raised edge case (a review's "what about scenario X?"), check whether the system's existing composed rules already produce the right answer — behaviour that emerges from a composition of independent rules (a pure reducer, a set of matchers) is often already covered, sometimes on more than one independent count. When it is, add no production code: pin it with a regression test — and an accept criterion under the relevant requirement, where you track those — asserting the contrast case too, so the test would bite if the rule interaction ever changed.
74	- A bespoke how-to earns its place only by what it adds over authoritative external docs — our own failure modes, gotchas, and the exact path we ran. Before writing one, check it against those docs and keep only the additive parts; a guide that re-explains upstream (often less well) is worse than a link to upstream plus a short gotchas list. And document/recommend only a path you've actually run, not the "standard" or seemingly-better one you haven't.
75	- Resilience that swallows errors destroys observability — during development, before a solution is proven right, add debugging information first, and remove it later.
76	- A capability applied **best-effort behind a silent fallback** (a probe-gated optimisation, an optional hardware/platform feature, a hint the runtime may ignore) must **record whether it actually engaged** — read the state back where the platform exposes it, and log which path ran. Without that, every later measurement of the feature is uninterpretable: a session where it quietly never engaged looks exactly like one where it did and didn't help, so the data says nothing about the feature and a bug report about it can't be diagnosed. The fallback keeps the run alive; the record is what keeps it *evaluable*.
77	- Keep everything the software persists on a user's machine under **one** user-deletable location. "Delete that folder and it's gone" is a promise users act on — someone who deletes it believes the whole record went with it — so a new storage need extends that location rather than earning a second one, and anything the platform forces outside it (a registration the OS owns) is named explicitly as the exception.
78	- A user-facing statement about what the software does with a user's data — a permission prompt's usage string, a privacy policy, a store-listing disclosure — is part of the behaviour's contract, not documentation of it. Change the behaviour and the statement changes **in the same commit**; a stale disclosure is worse than a blunt one. And read the direction the other way too: retaining something previously not retained, adding an outbound connection, or opening a listener is a change to the *promise*, not a new field — it earns an explicit decision, and the disclosure rewrite, before the code. Expect the claim to live in **more than one place** — the same absolute is typically restated in a page's `<meta>` description, a marketing lede, a README and a source-file header, and nothing fails when a change makes one of them untrue. Grep the whole surface for the standing absolutes a behaviour change touches ("no tracking", "no cookies", "no external assets") and reconcile every hit in that same commit.
79	- When a session will drive an external runtime more than once (a headless browser, a device, a REPL, a deploy target), write **one** parameterised driver script into the scratchpad and re-point it — take the target, the selector, and the output path from argv — rather than authoring a fresh throwaway per invocation. A re-run costs seconds; re-authoring costs 15–20 s each and re-derives the same setup every time, which is where a surprising share of a long session's wall clock goes.
80	- When automating a task that requires live AI conversation context (e.g., a reflection pass over a session), hook it to an existing human workflow event rather than background infrastructure — shell hooks lack conversation access and fire at per-turn granularity, not session-end. The cheapest trigger is often a change to an existing command's definition.
81	- In a pipeline or CI workflow, treat expected, handled outcomes (known-bad inputs, anticipated stops) as clean exits with a comment — not failures. Reserve the failure signal for genuine breakage; a red run should always be a surprise.
82	- A live fetch that works on your machine can fail from CI or a sandbox (403/400, a CAPTCHA wall) because the *datacenter IP* is blocked, not the User-Agent — browser-like headers won't change that. Route the fetch through a residential-proxy service (these usually render JS too, so a single-page app records real content) rather than tweaking headers; treat targets that stay blocked even through a proxy as un-cacheable.
83	- `pkill -f "<pattern>"` matches the *invoking shell's own* command line too, so a pattern naming the process you want also names the shell that typed it — the shell dies, and everything chained after the `pkill` (`;`, `&&`) is silently dropped, with the run reporting only a bare non-zero exit. Never chain a `-f` pkill; and break the self-match by bracketing one character of the pattern (`pkill -f "[h]ttp.server 8099"`), which still matches the target but no longer matches the literal you just typed.
84	- A cloud/root setup script may start in the repo's *parent* directory, not the checkout — a bare `npm ci` / build there finds no manifest and silently does nothing, surfacing much later as a confusing missing-deps error. Make the setup script `cd` into the checkout before running anything.
85	- A `Cannot find module …` (or other missing-dependency) error on a *fresh* checkout almost always means the install hasn't run there yet, not a code bug — `node_modules` and other vendored dependency dirs start empty on a clone and on an ephemeral CI/sandbox checkout. Run the install and re-run before hunting for a code-level cause.
86	- Collapse a property tracked in more than one place (a spec tag, a side manifest, a per-item field) into a single source of truth, preferring a *structural* classifier — one derived from where the item lives (its folder or path) — over a hand-set field: a structural classifier has no field to forget to update and can't desync from the item it classifies.
87	- Avoid a default value; require it explicitly, or make it structural (derived from where the thing lives). A default moves the real value into a fallback (`x || DEFAULT`) plus a comment documenting it — two things that drift, neither visible at the call site — all to save a little typing. When automation maintains many instances of a config (a fleet of repos, generated project files), have the automation **materialize the explicit value into every file it maintains** instead of interpreting absence: the knob then sits visibly in the exact file where anyone would go to change it, and a missing key becomes drift the automation repairs rather than a case code must interpret (e.g. the fleet baselining writing `"maintenance": { "delivery": "auto" }` into each member's `.claudinite-checks.json`).
88	- **"Unknown" is a state of its own — never encode it as a zero, an empty string, or a type's default, and never let a decoder collapse it into one.** A field that can legitimately be absent carries three states, not two (absent, zero, a real value), and every stage of a pipeline has to preserve the distinction: encode unknown as a missing key or an explicit null, keep the zero for a real zero, and treat the absent case as a normal, permanent shape of the data rather than a gap something downstream should close. A stage that folds three states into two loses what nothing downstream can recover, and it fails silently — every value it emits is plausible. Where two fields make overlapping claims about the same fact (a `free` flag beside a `price: 0`), keep each meaning what its own source said and let the consumer decide.
89	- When a check that walks a file tree (an orphan/reachability scan, a doc audit, a lint) must ignore files you don't own — a synced submodule, a vendored dependency, generated output — derive its file set from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with a hardcoded path-to-skip. There's no exclude path to maintain, it can't desync when an artifact moves, and it stays correct when a new gitignored directory appears. Git already knows what you own; tracked vs. ignored is the exact distinction. The price of that precision: a *brand-new* file is untracked, so it sits outside the sweep until it is committed — the run's own "checked N files" line is **not** evidence your new file was among them. Commit (or `git add`) first, then re-run, before reading a green sweep as coverage of what you just wrote.
90	- A check that scans source for a forbidden token (a banned API, an impure import, a DOM specific) must match *code, not prose* — strip comments before you match, or a comment that merely names the token (`// saved in chrome.storage`) fails the build over an English sentence, and the next author who documents the very rule you're enforcing trips it. Strip *string-aware*: a `//` inside `"https://…"` is not a comment, and blindly deleting to end-of-line corrupts real code (and can hide a genuine violation later on that line). The corpus's reusable helper is `stripComments` in [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs); a project whose scan can't import it (e.g. a test that runs where the mount is absent) should inline the same string-aware pass and point a comment back at that canonical source.
91	- A comment describes the code's *current state*, never the edit that produced it. Don't explain the change you just made, and don't explain an absence — a comment saying something was removed, renamed, or "no longer" done describes a version of the file the reader can't see and doesn't need; the diff and the commit message are where change history belongs, and they keep it accurate without maintenance. State the reason the code is the way it is now, or write nothing. The same applies to a comment that narrates a fix in the past tense ("switched to X because Y broke"): keep only the part still true of the code in front of you ("X, because Y can't handle Z"), and drop the rest.
92	- Comments are not free: each one is a claim the next reader must verify against the code, and a claim that will drift. Add one only when it carries something the code cannot — more comments help only when each pays for itself, and a comment that restates the code costs attention while adding nothing.
93	- A comment should carry the *why* or a cross-file relationship the code can't state itself — not a fact already reconstructable from same-file code plus a known convention (a restated fact drifts out of sync as the code changes, silently). When a comment must name another file, state its exact path in exactly one canonical place and have every other mention point at that reference or the concept, not re-spell the path — a path repeated across many comments turns every future move into comment-churn the code itself never needed.
94

98	# claude-code-web-users-support — for the people working on this from the web
99	
100	A Claude Code **web** session runs for a signed-in person, in a managed container. A
101	terminal session does neither. This pack is where the capabilities that depend on that
102	difference live — anything a project can offer only when the session knows **who** is
103	here.
104	
105	## Personal interaction preferences
106	
107	This project reads each person's **personal interaction preferences** at session start:
108	how they want to be worked with — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, the
109	phrases they use to trigger a defined command. If the current user has a file in the
110	store, its contents are already in this session's context, injected under this pack's
111	marker by [`session-start.mjs`](session-start.mjs).
112	
113	**They are not project conventions.** Conventions belong to the packs that own each
114	subject and load as prose. What this carries is *personal*: the same rules travel with
115	a person across every project they work in, and two people on one project can want
116	different things. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project
117	convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the preference owns only the
118	trigger phrase.
119	
120	**The pack holds an address, not the content.** Preferences belong to a group of people
121	rather than to any one repository, so this project's declaration names the **store** —
122	a repo, and a path inside it holding one `<email>.md` per person:
123	
124	```json
125	{ "id": "claude-code-web-users-support", "config": { "repo": "owner/name", "path": "preferences" } }
126	```
127	
128	`path` is optional and defaults to `preferences`. Reading is **local-first**: when this
129	repo *is* the store, the working copy wins over the default branch, so an edit in
130	progress is what the session sees.
131	
132	**Every miss is fail-soft.** No identity (a terminal session has none), no configured
133	store, no file for this person, a fetch that fails — each is one plain-text note and the
134	session proceeds on default interaction behavior. Nothing here is load-bearing, and a
135	nice-to-have must never be able to stop a session from starting.
136	
137	### Adding or changing a preference
138	
139	Edit that person's file **in the store repo** — never here, and never in the canon. One
140	distilled preference per bullet, in the imperative: a preference is a rule the assistant
141	can act on, not a description of a mood. A preference that turns out to be a project
142	convention in disguise belongs in the pack that owns its subject instead.
143

147	# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy
148	
149	The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
150	pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
151	the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
152	([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
153	[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
154	[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).
155	
156	The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**
157	
158	- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
159	  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
160	  ref's auto-generated name.
161	- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
162	  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
163	  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
164	  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.
165	
166	Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
167	**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
168	rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
169	three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.

174	# Claudinite — the canon's own non-portable working rules
175	
176	This is the Claudinite home repo's own local pack: the capture surface for lessons that are
177	**specific to working on the canon itself** and would not make sense mounted into a consuming
178	project. Portable lessons — anything true for repos beyond this one — belong in the shared canon
179	under `packs/`/`skills/` instead (proposed by PR, or lifted by the promote stage).
180	
181	The growth lifecycle writes here automatically: the `growth-extract` daily task routes the canon's
182	own non-portable lessons — mined from repo activity and from captured conversations alike — into
183	this pack (each at the local promotion ladder's strongest mechanism — a check where the rule is deterministic, otherwise terse
184	prose below).
185	
186	## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate
187	
188	- **`canon-curation` lives in `.claudinite/local/packs/`, not `packs/`** (owner decision,
189	  2026-07-19). The canon home's curation duties are Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite —
190	  project-specific content on the home's own capture surface. Do not propose moving it back, and
191	  do not describe the move as open or provisional.
192	- **Local-pack `run_daily` scheduling is ON — the fleet's default path** (same decision). The
193	  planner reads every member's local-pack daily descriptors by default; never reintroduce an
194	  "experimental / not enabled" framing or an opt-in seam for it.
195	- **Packs-tree segregation is barriers configuration only.** Any rule about what the `packs/`
196	  tree may reference is expressed by declaring/configuring the `barriers` pack (contributed
197	  edges, `siblings`/`scope` capabilities — extend barriers generically if a capability is
198	  missing). Never write standalone code that checks packs-tree segregation.
199	- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` records the mechanism only** (owner decision, 2026-07-23,
200	  #420). Status, phase tracking, in-flight-PR reconciliation and remaining work live in that
201	  initiative's tracking issue (task-prework → #394); a phased plan lives in the sibling
202	  `MIGRATION.md`. Don't reintroduce a status / open-questions / remaining-work section there.
203	- **Multi-session work hands off through the tracking issue, never a prepared prompt** (owner
204	  correction, 2026-07-23). The owner's opener is `continue work on #<n>`, so state not written
205	  into the issue is lost. Before ending a session on unfinished work, update the issue and let
206	  the session summary be a pointer to it — never compose a bespoke "pick up from here" prompt.
207	- **The canon never knows which repos consume it — fleet-wide aggregation is Sheepdog's domain**
208	  (owner correction, 2026-07-28, #520). Designing anything that spans repos, the tempting shape is
209	  a member list (or a "fleet" task) living in the canon. It doesn't go here: the canon carries only
210	  **mechanisms exercised on itself**, and the knowledge of *which* repos exist stays in the
211	  **Sheepdog** repo and its pack, which enumerates members at runtime from its own
212	  `.claudinite-checks.json` entry — exactly where `fleet-census` and `fleet-freshness` already keep
213	  it. So a cross-repo feature splits in two: a self-contained per-repo half in the canon, and the
214	  aggregation half as a Sheepdog fleet task. **No repo list exists anywhere in canon code** — and a
215	  derived fleet artifact lands in Sheepdog as a daily **auto-merged PR of a `GENERATED` file**,
216	  never a direct commit to its `main`.
217	- **A pack default stays in the pack — don't ask it at adoption, don't write it into a member's
218	  config** (owner ruling, 2026-07-28, #527/#528). An adoption question whose recommended answer is
219	  right for nearly everyone is "bad noise": it taxes every adopting repo to re-state the default,
220	  and materializing that answer into `.claudinite-checks.json` freezes a copy that then drifts from
221	  the pack and has to be migrated. Keep the default in the pack's own code, ask nothing, and let the
222	  rare project that wants to differ add the setting by hand. Read config as *optional* — an unset
223	  key means "the default", never "misconfigured" (`retention_days` unset is precisely why the
224	  growth-extract retention prune is skipped rather than failing).
225	
226	- **What Claudinite ships must run on the credentials and settings a member already has**
227	  (owner ruling, 2026-08-06). Requiring a member to flip a platform setting, or to provision a wider
228	  credential (a PAT, an app installation, a new secret), is a last resort — not because it is hard,
229	  but because it is per-repo manual work that reliably does not happen: the capability is then
230	  quietly dead in every repo nobody configured, indistinguishable from a Claudinite bug, while the
231	  automation's own report says nothing is wrong. Three members filed issues asking for the same
232	  Actions approval setting (ClaudiniteWebsite#95, EdFringeNow#205, TLDR#182); none was changed, and
233	  each repo's converge kept succeeding while its mount fell a day behind. Prefer the route that
234	  works with the Action's own `GITHUB_TOKEN` and stock configuration even when it is less direct,
235	  and where a platform behaviour blocks you, neutralise its *effect* rather than asking for the
236	  platform to be reconfigured. Where no such route exists — a capability the default credential
237	  cannot hold at all, which is why `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` is legitimate — take the requirement
238	  deliberately: name the exact scope, say why nothing weaker suffices, and have the automation
239	  report when it is missing rather than silently degrading.
240	
241	- **A change to what members receive is not verified until a member has received it — force that in
242	  the same session** (owner requirement, 2026-08-06: *"We're not waiting till tomorrow to see if
243	  something worked"*). Merging to canon is evidence about canon; the only thing that exercises a
244	  canon change end to end is a member's converge, and on a daily slot that is a day away — so a
245	  session that closes on "it reaches the fleet tonight" has shipped an unverified change and hands
246	  the owner a question they will ask anyway (asked five separate ways across 2026-08-05/06:
247	  *"Check status"*, *"Did the Sheepdog baselining work?"*, *"check now"*, *"How do you know 'the
248	  fleet is now fully on 076c029'?"*, and forced baselines appended to three consecutive `lgtm`s).
249	  After landing anything that alters what baselining delivers, drive Sheepdog's `fleet-baseline`
250	  workflow with `follow` and report what it did per member, unasked. Two corollaries. **A dispatch
251	  is not a result** — the API's 204 means queued. And **attaching a member repo to the session is a
252	  read you already have**, so attach the repos the verification needs rather than offering to: *"2
253	  of 11 members confirmed … say the word and I'll attach and verify"* bought a round-trip, one of
254	  four the owner spent that morning telling this session to attach repos.
255	
256	- **A code deprecation rides the standard `@deprecated` tag — never a bespoke conformance check**
257	  (owner ruling, 2026-08-09, #707). Retiring a field, option or module does not earn its own rule
258	  module, test file and catalog row: that is machinery to say what one JSDoc line says, and it grows
259	  once per retirement forever. `deprecated-session-scope` was authored as a `basics` check and deleted
260	  the same day it was reviewed (*"I don't think we want to add a check for every code deprecation"*).
261	  Put `@deprecated` on the **definition** — the one place the thing is declared, here the
262	  `session_scope` section of `engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs` — and have each sanctioned holdout
263	  pacify the warning with a comment at its own declaration site saying why it still carries the field.
264	  Keep the contract **validating** the lingering field either way: validation catches a typo that would
265	  otherwise strand a dispatch, and is not the same thing as a conformance rule.
266	
267	## Canon-specific gotchas
268	
269	- **Baselining backfill skips the home.** The nightly baselining that lands a `seededByDefault`
270	  pack (and canon-delivered declaration changes) on every member is gated `!isHome`, so the canon
271	  home is the one repo it never reaches: what the fleet receives automatically, this repo's own
272	  `.claudinite-checks.json` only ever gets by hand.
273	- **Pack discovery imports the whole pack tree eagerly — declaration is irrelevant.**
274	  `discoverPacks` imports every `packs/<name>/pack.mjs` on disk and `scanSkillChecks` imports
275	  every `<pack>/skills/<skill>/checks.mjs` beside it, *before* activation is consulted. So
276	  anything in that import graph loads in every repo under every declaration, and a module that is
277	  also a CLI entry point gets re-imported while it is still evaluating: a top-level `await` in its
278	  entry block then never settles and Node exits 13 having run nothing (#581 — `interview.mjs
279	  check` deadlocked fleet-wide, invisible because the SessionStart orchestrator's fail-soft reads
280	  it as a merely-absent note). Start the work *after* evaluation completes — `check(…).catch(…)`.
281	  Enforced by `pack-discovery-entry-await`; the corollary it can't check is to keep these modules
282	  import-light in the first place.
283	- **A pack's `RULES.md` is injected into every session that declares the pack — an idea nobody can
284	  act on belongs in `docs/`, and a pack file must not link there.** Deferred directions, blocked
285	  proposals and status live in `docs/` (e.g. `docs/future-directions.md`) precisely because pack
286	  prose costs context in every consumer session. And the pointer cannot go the other way: `docs/`
287	  is outside the vendor set, so a link from any file under `packs/` resolves to nothing in every
288	  consumer — the `reference-integrity` class that reached `main` unnoticed in #424 (and that
289	  check is work-scoped, so it only sees paths the branch itself deletes). Reference `docs/` from
290	  the issue or PR instead.
291	- **A pack's `RULES.md` carries directives an agent must obey — never a walkthrough of how the
292	  feature works** (owner correction, 2026-08-06: *"Rules are context for any agentic work, not for
293	  random explanations"*). The same injection that makes the prose useful makes description
294	  expensive: a paragraph that only *describes* a mechanism is paid for by every session in every
295	  declaring repo and steers none of them. Shipping the fleet-baseline `follow` half, the rule the
296	  change actually added was one sentence — the two extra PAT read scopes a followed run needs —
297	  and everything around it was a feature tour. Behaviour description goes in the module header and
298	  the pack `README.md`, read by whoever works on that code rather than loaded ambiently; the test
299	  before a paragraph goes in is whether an agent could *act* differently for having read it. Same
300	  instinct as the comment rule `basics` now carries (describe the current state, not the change),
301	  applied where the cost is per session rather than per reader.
302	- **Pick a scheduled task's cadence from how often its signal actually moves.** On a member the
303	  mounted canon changes most nights — baselining converges `.claudinite/shared/` daily — so any
304	  precondition reading `sharedMount` fires nearly every night, spending an opus dispatch per
305	  firing. Where the work isn't latency-sensitive (pruning, dedup), a stale item stays harmlessly
306	  correct, so daily buys noise, not freshness: `growth-dedup` moved to `weekly` in #583 and loses
307	  nothing, because the signals are window-scoped (`sinceIso`) and `windowStart` widens to the
308	  widest due task's period — a weekly run sees all 7 days, batched rather than dropped.
309	- **The home doesn't declare `git-github`, so its skills never mount — never conclude "no such
310	  skill" from `.claude/skills/`.** `mount-skills.mjs` filters on the *literal* declaration
311	  (`isActive(p, { packs: declared })`), not the `requires` closure `check_the_world.mjs` resolves,
312	  and the baselining that would normalize that closure into `.claudinite-checks.json` is the one
313	  thing gated `!isHome` — so `merge-to-main` and `git-github-advanced` are simply absent here.
314	  Read `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` out of the tracked tree — the corpus *is* this repo,
315	  and an unmounted skill says nothing about whether its procedure applies. The seeding gap above
316	  is a different one (`git-github` arrives by closure, never `seededByDefault`); catching this
317	  one needs `resolveDeclaredPacks` compared against the literal declaration.
318	- **The same blindness on the member side: a session sees only the packs its repo *declares*, so never
319	  conclude from the mount that no canon pack owns a lesson.** A member's `.claudinite/shared/packs/`
320	  holds its declared set, not the canon — so a pack the repo doesn't declare is simply absent, and the
321	  honest-looking reading ("nothing here covers this") is wrong in the one direction that costs most:
322	  the lesson gets homed in a **new local pack** on the member, duplicating canon territory. Measured
323	  2026-08-09 on EdFringeNow: the client-side data-caching rules that belonged to `static-website` went
324	  into a fresh local pack (whose `ruleRoutingGuidance.belongs` ran 31 words against the 20-word cap, so
325	  the session's own selftest was red), because the repo carries no `site.config` and doesn't declare
326	  the pack — nothing in the session pointed at it. The owner did, by URL: *"That pack does exist … move
327	  the changes into that pack and cleanup the EdFringeNow rules."* Since #728 every mount carries
328	  `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`, the catalog of **every** canon pack — read that, not the mounted
329	  subset, before homing a lesson locally. And when the owning pack's territory is merely too narrow,
330	  **widen its `belongs`** rather than route around it: #727 widened `static-website` by two words,
331	  "shipping" → "shipping and serving", and the rules landed where they belonged. (Portable — a promote
332	  candidate for `grow_with_claudinite/extracting-lessons.md`, whose "route to the pack whose territory
333	  owns it" step assumes that pack is visible from the session.)
334	- **Never re-serialize a repo's JSON config to apply an edit — patch the text.** A round-trip
335	  rewrites what it wasn't asked to: Python's `json.dump` defaults to `ensure_ascii=True` (every
336	  non-ASCII character becomes a `\uXXXX` escape), and indent, key order and the trailing newline
337	  become the serializer's opinion. Nothing fails and tests stay green, so it rides onward. Edit
338	  JSON as anchored text; if you must round-trip, pin every lossy default and read the resulting
339	  diff before committing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `repo-text-sweeps`, where a
340	  `\uXXXX`-in-tracked-JSON check would carry it.)
341	- **Test git fixtures must commit with signing off.** `engine-tests/helpers.mjs`'s `makeRepo`
342	  overrides identity but not signing, so all 31 call sites route fixture commits through the
343	  signing service; when it degrades, each commit blocks on it and the suite leaks descriptors
344	  (~800 per full run against a 4096 cap) until `git commit` and `git push` fail process-wide.
345	  Commit with `git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit --no-gpg-sign`: signing a tmpdir throwaway
346	  buys nothing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `writing-tests`.)
347	- **A canon session with a consumer repo also in its sources will reach for the *consumer's*
348	  merge skill — merge by the skill of the repo you are merging into.** Canon work is routinely
349	  dual-repo (the canon plus the fleet member being piloted), and both repos ship a merge skill
350	  under different names — the canon's `packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/` and, say, GCEC's
351	  local `merge-and-ci`. The consumer's skill wins the match on name/description and is followed
352	  to the letter, so the canon-only steps in *its* recipe are silently skipped — repeatedly, the
353	  **post-merge conversation capture** (`node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue
354	  <n>`, the "After the merge" section of `merge-to-main`). So: before merging in a dual-repo
355	  session, resolve the merge skill **by target repo**, not by which skill matched first — and
356	  treat capture as part of the merge, not as an optional epilogue.
357	- **Fail-soft SessionStart steps hide their own breakage fleet-wide — test the emitted
358	  output, not the exit code.** Every `engine/pack_loader/` SessionStart step
359	  (`inject-pack-prose.mjs`, `mount-skills.mjs`, `env-requirements.mjs`) wraps its body in
360	  `try { ... } catch {}` so a broken loader never blocks a session. That fail-soft is deliberate,
361	  but it means a runtime fault — a wrong dynamic-import target, a renamed module — exits 0 and
362	  simply emits nothing: no error, no signal. And because the engine is vendored verbatim into
363	  every member, one canon regression silently disables that step across the whole fleet at once.
364	  So a step like this must be guarded by a regression test that runs the real script against a
365	  real corpus and asserts the **positive** effect — prose IS emitted — never merely that
366	  `status === 0` (which fail-soft makes meaningless); see
367	  `engine-tests/pack_loader/inject-pack-prose.test.mjs`.
368	- **The nightly self-refresh cannot repair the vendor-set computation — pin operational
369	  files against the REAL canon tree.** Baselining's converge re-runs
370	  `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.mjs` from canon HEAD, so a bug *in that computation* is
371	  the one class of canon regression that is not self-healing: every refresh faithfully
372	  reproduces it, and recovery is an out-of-band vendor refresh applied to each member by
373	  hand. So when the vendor set excludes by *pattern*, an operational file that matches
374	  needs a by-path whitelist (`VENDORED_ENGINE_DOCS`) **and** a regression test asserting
375	  against the real canon tree, not only a synthetic fixture: a fixture keeps proving the
376	  whitelist mechanism works while the live path silently drops out from under it (see the
377	  paired tests in `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.test.mjs`).
378	- **A check that selects its inputs by path pattern can reach zero files and still pass — assert
379	  the live in-scope count.** When skills moved inside their owning pack (#385),
380	  `skill-no-enforcement-narration` kept scanning the root-level `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` layout: it
381	  matched nothing in any tree, read as live, and caught nothing until a human noticed the prose it
382	  should have flagged (#560 — 21 skills in scope once repointed). Its fixtures are why it hid so
383	  well; they spelled the same dead layout, so five green tests proved the *matching* and never the
384	  *selection*. A scan-based check therefore needs one assertion over the **real** tree that its
385	  scope is non-empty. Other half of the same class: agent-facing text pointing where the code isn't
386	  — the same PR fixed a rule whose `why`, fix text and `doc` all named `engine/checks_helpers` or
387	  `checks/lib`, neither of which ever existed. Nothing catches that on its own —
388	  `reference-integrity` is work-scoped and flags only paths the branch itself deletes — so grep the
389	  tree for any directory you name in a finding, a remedy, or a doc pointer before shipping it.
390	- **A scheduled task's precondition gates on movement in the window, never on standing state.** "An
391	  open PR exists" is true forever once it is true once, so the task wakes every night, spends an
392	  agent, and re-derives yesterday's verdict over an unchanged set (three of tidy-repo's tasks
393	  shipped that way; fixed in #554). Gate on the objects' own movement — a `touched` list or a
394	  tip-commit date, which the signal collector has to actually carry (`branches` carried names only,
395	  so "is any of this new" had no answer at all). A signal that is true most days on an active repo
396	  — a substantive `main` move — may only **widen** an already-triggered run, never wake one. And the
397	  gate is not the scope: where a verdict is relative to the rest of the set (superseded-by,
398	  already-in-`main`), newness gates and the full set stays the scope. (Portable — a promote
399	  candidate for `basics/scheduled-tasks.md`, which states the precondition contract but not this.)
400	- **You cannot force a due slot by running the scheduler workflow by hand.** Dueness is
401	  stateless — a slot is due iff its time falls in `(last successful run, now]` — so a
402	  `workflow_dispatch` run outside the slot's window succeeds, prints `- no tasks due`, and
403	  does nothing. It looks like a healthy run. To exercise a task Action-side, invoke its
404	  worker directly, or move the slot hour in `taskScheduler` and wait for the cron.
405	- **A scheduled task is gated twice — prove a change through `planRun`, never through its own
406	  precondition.** `planRun` computes the due list *before* any precondition runs, so a task whose
407	  most-recent slot has already been run is never evaluated and never reads its signals at all. #513's
408	  forced-run override landed with every test driving the precondition (or the signal collector) directly
409	  and was inert on exactly the run it existed for — the mid-day manual trigger — because the due-list
410	  gate it never touched had already dropped the task (`evaluations: []`; fixed in #516). A test that
411	  starts *inside* the gate proves only "works once evaluated" and says nothing about whether the task
412	  ever gets there. Drive the real `planRun` from a deliberately **non-due** slot: that is the only shape
413	  that catches it.
414	- **Every due task in a run shares ONE checkout — an agentless worker must not touch it.** The
415	  scheduler runs the whole due list in a single working tree, so a worker that checks out a branch or
416	  leaves an index behind hands the next task a tree it did not expect, and a run that dies leaves the
417	  mess for whatever follows. A task whose output is a regenerated file lands it through
418	  `engine/scheduler/deliver-generated.mjs` — git plumbing against the fetched base tip, with HEAD, the
419	  index and the working tree untouched — and reads its prior state from that base rather than local
420	  HEAD, so stacked runs stay idempotent. (`basics/baselining`'s own deliver is the deliberate
421	  exception: it commits a whole working tree and re-cuts a dated family branch; the landing itself —
422	  delivery preference, CI dispatch, arm/land/merge — is shared, in `engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs`.)
423	- **A code-search hit is evidence; a code-search miss is not — survey by reading each file.**
424	- **Derive the test file list from the tree — every hand-written glob here under-runs the suite.**
425	  There is no `package.json` and no test script, so each session invents its own incantation and
426	  silently verifies less than it thinks. Measured in this checkout: `node --test <dir>` does not
427	  recurse — it resolves the path as a module and dies with `Cannot find module`; bash `**` is not
428	  recursive without `globstar`, so `engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs` reaches
429	  **37 of 65** tracked test files. Four consecutive sessions (2026-07-26, #459/#452/#435/#468) each
430	  wrote a different command and reported 587, 690, 621 and 697 tests — three of them pushed after
431	  running a strict subset. Neither published list is authoritative either: `ci.yml`'s `tests=(…)`
432	  array omits `vendoring/*.test.mjs`, and `engine/checks/README.md`'s "as CI runs it" one-liner
433	  names `engine/test/`, `skills/` and `mount/`, none of which exist. So enumerate from git and let
434	  the count speak: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. (The drift-guard, once the array is
435	  clean: assert every tracked `*.test.mjs` is matched by `ci.yml`'s globs.)
436	- **A branch that waited overnight has lost its base *and* possibly its premise — re-verify the
437	  problem still exists on current `main`, unasked.** This repo merges its own scheduled-task PRs
438	  without a human, on top of multi-phase migrations that retire whole directories: measured on
439	  PR #465, `main` moved **14 commits in 13.7 hours** and one of them (#473, "retire `run_daily/`")
440	  *deleted the file the PR's diagnosis rested on* and had already landed most of its content. The
441	  branch rebased cleanly and the tests stayed green — the change was simply no longer the change to
442	  make, and the correct move was `git checkout -B <branch> origin/main` and re-applying only the
443	  surviving slice (9 files → 2). So syncing the base is not the check; the check is a **content**
444	  one: after `git fetch`, read what the new commits did to the surface you are changing and state
445	  whether the problem is still there, what the goal was, and what survives. Do this whenever you
446	  return to a paused branch, before presenting it — the owner should never have to ask "is this
447	  change still needed" (asked three times on #465 before it was volunteered).
448	- **Every `Claude_Code_Remote` call costs minutes, and a call that returns nothing has NOT failed —
449	  never re-issue it.** The whole server behaves this way, not one tool: measured over four sessions
450	  on 2026-07-29, `add_repo` ran 270–285s a call, `send_later` 117–390s, `list_triggers` 139–325s,
451	  `delete_trigger` 286–301s, `subscribe_pr_activity` 14–237s. They read like cheap registrations,
452	  so a session issues one, sits through minutes of silence, concludes it hung, and issues it again —
453	  and *the duplicate is the dominant cost*, because the first call had already succeeded:
454	  **#562 (`2026-07-29T1500Z`) — 6 `add_repo` calls, 1121s of that session's 1391s of tool
455	  wall-clock (81%)**, with `HelloWorldFlutterApp` added twice (285s + 271s); **#553
456	  (`2026-07-29T2206Z`) — the same PR check-in `send_later`d 4 times, 1107s of 2028s (55%)**; **#544
457	  (`2026-07-29T1248Z`) — `list_triggers` ×2, `delete_trigger` ×2 on one trigger id, `send_later` ×2:
458	  1854s of 2472s (75%)**, in a session whose real work was 166 tool calls. `AskUserQuestion` shares
459	  the shape — #559's session asked one question twice for 218s + 204s. So: **one call per intent,
460	  ever**, and when what you want is "is it green yet", read the check status directly and merge on
461	  the already-green result rather than buying a notification. Budget these calls before making them:
462	  four of them is most of an hour.
463	- **Sync local `main` with `git reset --hard origin/main`, never `git pull` — this repo's session
464	  clones are shallow.** The post-merge sync step of `merge-to-main` is where it bites, and it bit
465	  five separate sessions on 2026-07-29 alone (#548, #551, #537, #559 and the session-end capture of
466	  `73a4db48`). A shallow clone has no common ancestor with the fetched remote, so `git pull` either
467	  demands an explicit strategy or reports the stale local ref as carrying unique commits it does not
468	  have — and the tempting reading, "local `main` has work the remote lacks", is wrong every time:
469	  the session's own work is already *in* `origin/main`, which is why it just merged. #537's session
470	  spent 87s across `git pull`, `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` and log comparisons proving
471	  that from scratch; #559's landed on "git sees no common ancestor" the same way. Nothing of value
472	  is ever on this repo's local `main`, so the sync is unconditional: `git fetch origin main && git
473	  reset --hard origin/main`. (Portable — a promote candidate for `git-github`'s merge procedure,
474	  where "your clone may be shallow" is true of any container-hosted session.)
475	- **The home has no `.claudinite/shared/` mount — machinery paths must accept both roots.** A
476	  consumer runs the vendored engine under `.claudinite/shared/engine/…` with packs under
477	  `.claudinite/(shared|local)/packs/…`; the home *is* the corpus and runs the same code from the
478	  repo root. So a path, regex, or workflow command written to the consumer mount shape works
479	  fleet-wide and fails on exactly this repo — the last place anyone exercises it, so the break
480	  surfaces late. Write the two-root form up front: make the `.claudinite/(shared|local)/` prefix
481	  optional in a pattern, and in a command probe for `.claudinite/shared/` first, falling back to
482	  the repo root.
483	- **Tightening a contract that member-owned files must satisfy has NO carrier — baseline
484	  migrations move paths, not schemas — so it lands as a fleet-wide silent break.** Vendoring
485	  refreshes `.claudinite/shared/` only; a member's `.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/pack.mjs` is
486	  the member's own content, which no converge may edit. And `migrations/` cannot help: its record
487	  is a path relocation (`aliases: [{ canonical, legacy }]`, applied by `applyFileAliases`), so it
488	  has no way to express "the field `rules` is now `worldRules`/`workRules`" or "`ruleRoutingGuidance`
489	  is now required" — exactly what #555 tightened, shipping no record because there was none to
490	  ship. The break is worse than loud: `normalizeManifest` returns `{ ...mod, rules }` with `rules`
491	  rebuilt **only** from the two scoped keys, so a legacy manifest's array is overwritten with `[]`
492	  and **that pack's checks simply stop running** — no error, the pack still loads. Measured on
493	  2026-07-30: **eleven local packs across ten of the thirteen members** had to be rewritten by
494	  hand in one session, and the members' own pack tests asserted `pack.rules` and went red on CI
495	  the moment the manifests moved. So before tightening anything a member's own file must satisfy,
496	  ask what carries it across the fleet; if the answer is "nothing", the change is not ready —
497	  accept the legacy shape in `normalizeManifest` (and say so) until a carrier exists, and never
498	  let a stale declaration degrade to *fewer checks running* rather than a failure.
499	- **A stub is copied once and never re-copied — extend its contract through an *optional* key, and let
500	  the declaration itself trigger the staleness check.** Vendoring refreshes `.claudinite/shared/`, but
501	  `packs/*/stubs/` are artifacts a member copied into its own `.github/` and no converge ever touches
502	  again — so a stub that learns to read a new config key is invisible to every repo still holding the
503	  old copy: the config names the key, the copied action ignores it, the run goes green, and the feature
504	  is silently dead in production. `build_vars` (#729) is the shape to copy. The key is **optional**, so
505	  no existing config is invalidated and no member has to be migrated to stay valid. A
506	  **declared-but-unset** value fails the run rather than exporting `""`, which would reproduce the same
507	  silent death one level down. And `release-workflows` flags exactly the combination that reads the key
508	  and ignores it — a config declaring it against an action or workflow copy predating the exporter — so
509	  the repos that opted in are told to re-copy and nobody else sees a finding. That pairing is the
510	  carrier the entry above asks for: an opt-in contract can ship without one only because declaring it
511	  is itself the signal a check can see.
512	- **A migration record is always the newest code; the engine that executes its result is the
513	  member's, and only as new as its last successful converge.** `migrations/apply.mjs` runs from a
514	  **fresh canon clone**, so every member gets today's record — but the worker that then commits and
515	  pushes it is the member's own **vendored** `.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/baselining/worker.mjs`,
516	  frozen at whatever converge last succeeded. So a record that needs a *new engine capability* to be
517	  deliverable is a **deadlock** on any member that hasn't got it yet: the record fires, the converge
518	  fails, the mount never advances — and the engine fix that would make the record deliverable can
